ENT Clinical Note – Teleconsultation  

Subjective:  
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure  
  • Intermittent episodes of right-hand pins-and-needles with transient limb weakness; no identifiable food, drug, or environmental trigger.  

- Symptom timeline and progression  
  • Onset ≈ 1½–2 months ago.  
  • Initial frequency: once per week to once per month; now occurring a couple of times per day.  
  • Each episode lasts several days, then resolves.  

- ENT symptoms  
  • During episodes: sensation of “something in my throat.”  
  • No throat tightness or feeling of airway closing.  
  • No voice change/hoarseness.  
  • No dysphagia or odynophagia (patient able to speak normally; drinking coffee only “slightly harder”).  
  • No drooling.  
  • No nasal or ocular symptoms.  
  • No stridor or other noisy breathing; no dyspnea.  
  • No swelling of lips, tongue, uvula, or face.  
  • No ear pain, hearing change, or neck pain/swelling.  

- Relevant past episodes and treatments  
  • First occurrence 1½–2 months ago; no prior ED visits or hospital admissions for these symptoms.  
  • No prior adrenaline/epinephrine or other acute treatments.  

- Allergies and current medications  
  • Allergy: penicillin.  
  • Medications: Aspirin 75 mg orally once daily (self-initiated).  

- Social context  
  • 32-year-old male; lives with wife; works as a plastic-surgery doctor; non-smoker.  

Objective:  
- Observable swelling: None reported/observed.  
- Airway/breathing: No stridor, no increased work of breathing documented.  
- Mental status: Alert, conversant; no dizziness or syncope noted during consultation.  
- Vitals and physical examination: Not recorded.  
- Accompaniment: Patient at home; wife lives with him (not present during call).  

Assessment:  
- Suspected transient ischemic attack (TIA) or mini-stroke (neurological origin) presenting with intermittent limb weakness/paresthesia; minimal ENT involvement (only transient throat sensation without objective airway compromise).  
- Justification: Recurrent focal neurological symptoms, family history of carotid disease/stroke, progression in frequency.  

Plan:  
- Immediate actions  
  • Urgent referral placed to rapid-access TIA clinic for carotid Doppler, brain imaging, and further work-up (expected appointment within 1–2 days).  

- Patient instructions  
  • If symptoms recur and are prolonged or worsen (persistent weakness, speech/swallowing difficulty, airway compromise, new visual loss), attend Emergency Department immediately.  
  • May contact GP service for interim guidance; clinic phone numbers (PALS and TIA service) placed in record for patient to chase appointment.  

- Escalation criteria / red flags emphasized  
  • Sudden trouble speaking, swallowing, or breathing.  
  • New or worsening throat tightness, voice change, facial/tongue swelling, stridor, or dyspnea.  
  • Persistent or worsening neurological deficits.  

- Follow-up  
  • Await TIA clinic assessment results.  
  • Review aspirin use after specialist evaluation.  
  • No specific ENT follow-up required unless new airway or swallowing issues develop.  

Quality checks (document_quality):  
• Missing but expected elements:  
  – No vital signs, cranial nerve exam, or airway examination documented.  
  – No detailed allergy list beyond penicillin; no prior anaphylaxis plan or auto-injector status (not clinically indicated but routinely checked in ENT allergy cases).  

• Internal conflicts: None noted.  

• Transcript quality: Moderate; occasional audio dropouts but clinically relevant information captured.
